newsitem.title: DENMARK: Trucker blockade not affecting Copenhagen - police.
newsitem.headline: Trucker blockade not affecting Copenhagen - police.

text.p: Danish police said on Wednesday there was no sign of a threatened blockade of the capital by protesting truckers and drivers leaders appeared divided on the issue.
"There is no sign of any unusual concentration of truck traffic on access roads to Copenhagen. Traffic in and out of the capital is normal," a police spokesman told Reuters.
The drivers, who have already sealed off the land border with Germany and blocked most seaports threatened on Tuesday to block roads into Copenhagen on Wednesday morning.
The Danish protest, against government plans to cut drivers' overseas subsistence allowances, was not related to French drivers' nationwide roadblock protests this week.

A drivers spokesman in Copenhagen said that up to 60 truckers in the capital were on standby to take action on orders from strike headquarters at the Padborg German border crossing in western Denmark.
But spokesman Ole Prusse, speaking to the Danish news agency Ritzau in Padborg said that his colleagues did not wish to hit commuter traffic in the capital.
"We won't blockade (Copenhagen). We don't want to hit private car traffic. We intend to keep our action on a sober level," Prusse said.

At a meeting in Padborg the truck drivers rejected on Wednesday an offer of a 100 crown rise in their daily overseas subsistence allowance to 250 crowns from Danish Tax Minister Carsten Koch and vowed to continue their three-day old action.
"It looks like we will be staying here with our trucks," Prusse said.

Some 1,500 Danish drivers have blocked goods traffic from crossing the land border with Germany since Monday and on Tuesday they broadened the blockade to most ports, halting exports to Norway and Sweden, radio reports said.
Freight traffic from the North Sea port of Esjberg to Britain was also affected.

Trapped at the Padborg crossing point on the Danish-German border were nearly a million Christmas trees in danger of rotting, along with major shipments of milk, cheese and meat, producers' organisations said.
The Danish post office said that international mail and post between the Danish islands and the Jutland peninsula were subject to delays.
